text:
Programming languages DO matter, just not necessarily for the reasons people think
Experienced
People often say "programming languages don't matter," meaning a good dev should be able to pick up anything. I agree—up to a point. But there's a big nuance people miss: how well do you actually know the domain?

Think of it this way:

If you’re a backend dev switching from Node to Go, you're learning new syntax, but you already know how APIs work. It's an easy transition.

If you’re a Node dev staying in TypeScript but switching to infrastructure automation, you already know the language, so you can focus entirely on learning the new domain.

But if you’re a Node dev switching to Go for infrastructure work, you're learning the syntax, the domain, and the tools all at once. That's a massive hurdle. It's like trying to cross greased monkey bars.

The ramp-up time is way longer when you're learning both the language and the concepts, which is why I don't buy the blanket "languages don't matter" claim.

What about AI? Some say it makes the language irrelevant since it can write code for you. AI is great for syntax, but if you don't understand the domain, how can you even tell if the code it's giving you is actually good? Just because it runs doesn't mean it's the right way to build it.

AI can help you write code, but it doesn't automatically mean you know how to check if that code is right.

My main point:

I think developers need some kind of solid foundation to start with.

If the language is new, knowing the concepts helps.

If the concepts are new, knowing the language helps.

But if both are new, the learning curve gets a lot steeper.

I'm not saying developers can't learn a new language and a new domain at the same time. Obviously, they can.

I'm saying employers need to account for that extra learning time instead of expecting the same productivity and onboarding speed as someone who already knows the language or the domain.

So maybe "programming languages don't matter" is a bit of an oversimplification.

Maybe a better way to put it is:

"Programming languages matter less when the underlying concepts are familiar."

I'm curious what other engineers think. Have you ever had to jump into a project where both the language and the domain were new to you? How did that affect how long it took to get up to speed?
label: market_take

text:
We scanned 3.5 million hosts for exposed .git repos and walked away with 400 AWS keys
Leaving a .git directory exposed is an old mistake with a single well known path, so we wanted to know how many organisations still make it. We pulled hostnames from certificate transparency logs, scanned 3.5 million live hosts, and found 28,000 repositories sitting wide open. 

400 AWS access keys came out of them, including one with access to a bucket of internal employment records, attendance logs and disciplinary files. Many of the credentials we pulled were still active when we tested. We disclosed them where we could find a contact.

Tom Steer, one of our security consultants, wrote up what we found and how gitreaper works, the tool we built to walk a repo's whole commit history in memory rather than writing 28,000 repositories to disk. That's also why we caught secrets in files that had been removed in later commits, which is often where the worst of it is.

Exposed .git is one of many thousands of issues that could be sitting on the internet waiting for someone to find them. We write custom Nuclei checks for that sort of thing and report them as vulnerabilities in Intruder, so it turns up in your scan results with the remediation advice attached.

Full write-up: We found 28,000 .git repos sitting wide open. Here's what was inside
